title: Reporting the model and the estimator
summary: Another researcher should be able to rebuild your model and rerun your estimation exactly from what you report.

body.text: Report the specification and the estimation choices completely (Hair et al. 2019; Appelbaum et al. 2018):

items: A diagram with all constructs, indicators and paths, and the hypotheses on the paths.
For each construct: reflective or composite-formative, and why.
Method and estimand: classic PLS (composites), PLSc (common factors via PLS) or CB-SEM; for CB-SEM the estimator (ML, MLR), the identification (marker or std-lv) and the missing-data method.
PLS settings: weighting scheme, iteration limit, tolerance, convergence.
Inference: bootstrap draws, seed, interval type (percentile), confidence level, one- or two-sided.
Software and versions: SEM Lab and its engine version, or the R/Python packages of an export.

body.text: SEM Lab writes a method statement with every run that contains most of these items. Check and edit it; it does not know why you chose reflective measurement or which hypotheses were directional.

mistake.title: "We used SmartPLS/SEM Lab" as the whole method section
mistake.text: The software name tells readers nothing about the estimand, the settings or the inference. Two analyses in the same program can differ in every one of them.

tryIt.task: Run the TAM example and open the method statement on the Results page. List any item from this lesson that it does not cover.

checks.question: Which detail is most important to add to "Paths were tested with bootstrapping (p < .05)"?

options.text: The number of draws, the seed, the interval type and whether tests were one- or two-sided.
options.feedback: Correct. These determine and reproduce the inference.

options.text: The colour of the arrows in the diagram.
options.feedback: Layout and colours are not part of the analysis.
Bootstrap results depend on B, the seed and the interval method.

checks.question: Why should a PLS report say whether classic PLS or PLSc was used?

options.text: They target different estimands (composites versus common factors) and give different numbers.

options.feedback: Neither is better in general; they answer different questions.

options.text: It does not matter for reflective models.
options.feedback: It matters most for reflective models, where PLSc changes loadings and paths.
